entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a sinusoid's amplitude and phase into the fixed t=0 complex phasor that anchors its later rotation and axis projections.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Phasors at Initial Time
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the initial phasor as the fixed $t=0$ complex snapshot whose magnitude is amplitude and whose angle is phase.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to convert $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ into the fixed initial phasor at $t=0$ by reading amplitude as magnitude and phase as angle.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the zero-phase case $A\cos(\omega t)$ first so the phasor sits on the positive real axis with angle $0$.
paragraph_plan: Define the initial phasor as the complex value attached to a sinusoid at $t=0$ and explain that it is the starting point for later rotation.
Show the zero-phase base case and connect amplitude to magnitude, so the phasor is just a positive real number when $\phi=0$.
Generalize to arbitrary phase by writing the same object in exponential form as $Ae^{j\phi}$.
Translate that exponential form into rectangular form with real part $A\cos\phi$ and imaginary part $A\sin\phi$.
Close by previewing that later lessons will rotate the same phasor and project it onto axes.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the scope at $t=0$ only; do not introduce time evolution, rotation direction, or axis projections beyond a one-sentence preview.

sections.section_title: Writing an Initial Phasor with Zero Phase
sections.learning_goal: Write a zero-phase sinusoid as an initial phasor on the positive real axis.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single-answer multiple choice; choose the equivalent initial phasor in compact complex form.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the initial phasor for $x(t)=9\cos(\omega t)$?
distractor_plan: Use a nonzero phase such as $9e^{j\pi/2}$ to catch students who ignore the zero-phase cue.
Use a purely imaginary option such as $9j$ to catch students who rotate the phasor by mistake.
Use a negative real option such as $-9$ to catch students who reverse the axis direction.
Use $0$ or an amplitude-only description to catch students who confuse phase zero with zero magnitude.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=6\cos(\omega t)$, write its initial phasor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that zero phase leaves the phasor on the positive real axis with magnitude equal to the amplitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the base case with no phase offset, so the only new action is to attach the amplitude to a real phasor at angle $0$.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude $6$ as the phasor magnitude.
Note that the phase is $0$, so the phasor angle is zero.
Write the phasor as $6e^{j0}$ and simplify it to $6$.
State that the result lies on the positive real axis.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude while keeping the phase exactly zero.
Use simple amplitudes that simplify directly to a real number.
Keep the frequency symbol irrelevant so the learner focuses only on the initial phasor.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the task purely as an initial-phasor write-off; do not introduce rotation or axis projection.

sections.section_title: Writing an Initial Phasor with Positive Phase
sections.learning_goal: Write a positive-phase sinusoid as an initial phasor with a positive angle.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single-answer multiple choice; choose the equivalent initial phasor in compact complex form.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the initial phasor for $x(t)=5\cos(\omega t+\pi/6)$?
distractor_plan: Drop the phase and give a real-axis answer.
Flip the phase sign and place the phasor in the lower half-plane.
Treat the phase as a magnitude and use $\pi/6$ as if it were the amplitude.
Use a purely imaginary option to catch students who confuse phase with a quarter-turn.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=8\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$, write its initial phasor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Preserve the positive phase as a counterclockwise angle while keeping amplitude as the magnitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with the zero-phase case, the only change is that the phasor now rotates into the upper half-plane.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude $8$ as the magnitude.
Read the positive phase $+\pi/3$ as the phasor angle.
Write the phasor as $8e^{j\pi/3}$.
If helpful, note the equivalent rectangular coordinates from $8\cos(\pi/3)$ and $8\sin(\pi/3)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the positive phase across simple angles such as $\pi/6$, $\pi/4$, and $\pi/3$.
Vary amplitude independently of phase so the learner must keep magnitude and angle separate.
Include phases that give clean rectangular components and phases that do not simplify as neatly.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the sign of the phase explicit; the student should see that positive phase means the initial phasor sits above the real axis.

sections.section_title: Writing an Initial Phasor with Negative Phase
sections.learning_goal: Write a negative-phase sinusoid as an initial phasor with a negative angle.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single-answer multiple choice; choose the equivalent initial phasor in compact complex form.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the initial phasor for $x(t)=7\cos(\omega t-\pi/6)$?
distractor_plan: Flip the sign of the phase and place the phasor above the real axis.
Ignore the phase sign and use a zero-angle answer.
Confuse magnitude and angle by making the amplitude equal to the phase.
Use a positive imaginary part to catch students who forget that a negative phase points downward.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=10\cos(\omega t-\pi/4)$, write its initial phasor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Translate the negative phase into a clockwise offset from the positive real axis without changing the amplitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the mirror image of the positive-phase case: the phasor still has the same magnitude, but it moves into the lower half-plane.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude $10$ as the magnitude.
Read the phase $-\pi/4$ as a negative angle.
Write the phasor as $10e^{-j\pi/4}$.
Optionally check the rectangular form to confirm the imaginary part is negative.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the negative phase across simple angles such as $-\pi/6$, $-\pi/4$, and $-\pi/3$.
Vary amplitude independently so the learner cannot rely on a memorized numeric pattern.
Include cases where the rectangular form lands in the lower half-plane.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign handling visible; the key error to prevent is losing the minus sign on the phase.

sections.section_title: Converting an Initial Phasor to Rectangular Form
sections.learning_goal: Convert an initial phasor from polar form to rectangular form by resolving its real and imaginary parts.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single-answer multiple choice; choose the rectangular complex number equivalent to the given initial phasor.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Convert the initial phasor $6e^{-j\pi/4}$ to rectangular form.
distractor_plan: Swap the real and imaginary parts.
Use the correct magnitude but the wrong sign on the imaginary part.
Leave the answer in exponential form instead of converting it.
Use the cosine value for both components or the sine value for both components.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert the initial phasor $8e^{j\pi/3}$ to rectangular form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use $Ae^{j\phi}=A\cos\phi+jA\sin\phi$ to compute the real and imaginary components.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same initial-phasor idea but adds one new task: turn the polar representation into explicit real and imaginary coordinates.
solution_step_plan: Start from the polar or exponential phasor form and identify $A$ and $\phi$.
Rewrite $e^{j\phi}$ as $\cos\phi+j\sin\phi$.
Evaluate the trig functions for the chosen angle.
Combine the results into rectangular form and simplify.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the angle across all quadrants so the learner must track the signs of both parts.
Use amplitudes that produce clean exact values as well as a few that need radical simplification.
Include phasors whose rectangular form has one zero component to test boundary cases.

sections.handoff_notes: Use the polar-to-rectangular conversion to reinforce the same initial-phasor rule from a different representation; do not introduce rotation over time.

entries.lesson_core_move: Track a phasor as uniform rotation in the complex plane by computing its instantaneous angle from initial phase and angular frequency.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Rotating Phasors
sections.learning_goal: Build the first model of a rotating phasor as a complex number with fixed magnitude and a time-varying angle $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the minimum rule for the lesson: the phasor's angle at time $t$ is the initial phase $\phi$ plus the rotation amount $\omega t$, so the instantaneous phasor is $Ae^{j(\phi+\omega t)}$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the simplest phasor, $A=1$ and $\phi=0$, so the learner sees that elapsed time alone produces the angle $\theta(t)=\omega t$ before adding a nonzero initial phase.
paragraph_plan: Define a rotating phasor as a complex number with fixed magnitude and an angle that advances uniformly with time.
State that the angle change over elapsed time is $\Delta\theta=\omega t$ and show the zero-phase base case.
Add the initial phase $\phi$ to obtain the instantaneous angle $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$.
Write the instantaneous phasor as $z(t)=Ae^{j\theta(t)}=Ae^{j(\phi+\omega t)}$.
Close by checking that $t=0$ returns the initial phasor $z(0)=Ae^{j\phi}$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the section fully symbolic and keep the explanation centered on the angle rule $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$. Do not introduce practice questions here.

sections.section_title: Computing Rotation Angle from Elapsed Time
sections.learning_goal: Compute the angle a phasor has rotated through after a given elapsed time by multiplying $\omega$ by $t$.

question_policy.answer_format: number (radians)
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor starts at angle $0$ and rotates at angular frequency $\omega=5$ rad/s. What angle has it rotated through after $t=2$ s?
distractor_plan: Use addition instead of multiplication, such as $\omega+t$.
Divide instead of multiply, such as $\omega/t$ or $t/\omega$.
Drop one factor from the product and return only $\omega$ or only $t$.
Make a small arithmetic slip in the product.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor starts at angle $0$ and rotates at angular frequency $\omega=2$ rad/s. What angle has it rotated through after $t=3$ s?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that elapsed rotation is $\Delta\theta=\omega t$ and evaluate it to get the angle after the given time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial established the rule $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$; this example removes the initial phase so the learner focuses only on the elapsed-time product.
solution_step_plan: Identify the angle change as $\Delta\theta=\omega t$.
Substitute the given angular frequency and elapsed time.
Multiply carefully and state the resulting angle in radians.
Note that because $\phi=0$, the instantaneous angle equals the rotation amount.
practice_variation_axes: Change the angular frequency and elapsed time.
Use a different exact or decimal elapsed time.
Ask for the angle after one or more full rotations worth of elapsed time.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the target on the scalar product $\omega t$. Do not add a nonzero initial phase until the next step.

sections.section_title: Adding Initial Phase to the Rotation Angle
sections.learning_goal: Combine initial phase and elapsed rotation to get the instantaneous angle $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor has initial phase $\phi=\pi/6$ and angular frequency $\omega=\pi$ rad/s. What is its instantaneous angle after $t=\tfrac{1}{2}$ s?
distractor_plan: Use only $\omega t$ and omit $\phi$.
Subtract the terms instead of adding them, such as $\phi-\omega t$.
Multiply the terms, such as $\phi\omega t$.
Combine the fractions of $\pi$ incorrectly or simplify to the wrong equivalent angle.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor has initial phase $\phi=\pi/3$ and rotates at angular frequency $\omega=2\pi$ rad/s. What is its instantaneous angle after $t=\tfrac{1}{4}$ s?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Substitute into $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$, compute the elapsed rotation, and simplify the sum to one angle.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example isolated elapsed rotation; this one adds a nonzero initial phase so the learner must combine the starting angle with the new rotation amount.
solution_step_plan: Write the instantaneous angle as $\theta(t)=\phi+\omega t$.
Substitute $\phi=\pi/3$, $\omega=2\pi$, and $t=\tfrac{1}{4}$.
Compute the rotation term $\omega t=\pi/2$.
Add the angles and simplify to $5\pi/6$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the initial phase.
Change the angular frequency or elapsed time so the product remains exact.
Require combining two fractional multiples of $\pi$.

sections.handoff_notes: The only new wrinkle is the nonzero initial phase. Keep the arithmetic on angle addition explicit.

sections.section_title: Writing the Instantaneous Phasor from Its Angle
sections.learning_goal: Convert an instantaneous angle into the complex phasor $Ae^{j\theta}$.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor has magnitude $A=2$ and angle $\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$. Which complex exponential represents it?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong sign in the exponent, such as $Ae^{-j\theta}$.
Keep the correct angle but change the magnitude.
Write a real-part or cosine form instead of the phasor form.
Use the right magnitude and a nearby but incorrect angle.

tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor has magnitude $A=3$ and instantaneous angle $5\pi/6$. Write the phasor in complex exponential form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize that a phasor with magnitude $A$ and angle $\theta$ is $Ae^{j\theta}$, then substitute the given values.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example found the angle; this one uses that angle to write the phasor itself.
solution_step_plan: Identify the magnitude $A$ and angle $\theta$ from the prompt.

sections.section_title: Reducing a Phasor Angle After Full Rotations
sections.learning_goal: Reduce an angle by subtracting full $2\pi$ turns while recognizing that the phasor does not change.

question_policy.answer_format: expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor has angle $\theta=13\pi/3$. Which angle is equivalent in $[0,2\pi)$?
distractor_plan: Subtract the wrong number of full turns.
Leave the angle outside the requested interval.
Use a negative coterminal angle when a positive reduced angle is requested.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor has angle $11\pi/3$. Reduce it to an equivalent angle in $[0,2\pi)$ and write the corresponding phasor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use periodicity to subtract the correct number of full rotations and express the same phasor with a smaller equivalent angle.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example wrote the phasor from a single angle; this one normalizes an angle that is larger than one full turn.
solution_step_plan: Recall that angles differing by multiples of $2\pi$ give the same phasor.
Subtract one full turn to move the angle into the requested range.
Check that the reduced angle is equivalent to the original angle.
Write the phasor using the reduced angle.
practice_variation_axes: Use angles larger than $2\pi$.
Use angles that reduce to a simple fraction of $\pi$.
Ask for the reduced angle only or for the equivalent phasor form.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the emphasis on periodic equivalence, not on changing the phasor itself. The learner should see that only the angle representation changes.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify phasor rotation as counterclockwise or clockwise by using the sign of angular frequency to determine the direction of phase progression.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Counterclockwise and Clockwise Rotation
sections.learning_goal: Establish that the sign of $\omega$ in $\theta(t)=\omega t+\phi$ determines whether phase angle increases or decreases with time, and therefore whether the phasor rotates counterclockwise or clockwise.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the sign rule for phasor rotation: positive $\omega$ makes the phase angle increase and the phasor rotate counterclockwise, while negative $\omega$ makes the phase angle decrease and the phasor rotate clockwise.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the unit phasor $e^{j\omega t}$ with $\phi=0$ so the only moving part is the sign of $\omega$.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the phase angle $\theta(t)=\omega t+\phi$ and frame rotation direction as the direction in which that angle changes over time.
Show that over a small positive time increment, the angle change has the same sign as $\omega$.
Explain that a positive $\omega$ makes the angle increase, which produces counterclockwise motion.
Explain that a negative $\omega$ makes the angle decrease, which produces clockwise motion.
Close by stating that initial phase $\phi$ only sets the starting angle and does not change the direction.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction tightly focused on the sign of $\omega$. Do not move into projections, cosine/sine recovery, or frequency components.

sections.learning_goal: Classify a phasor with positive angular frequency as counterclockwise and ignore the initial phase once the sign of $\omega$ is known.

Rewrite the same case as $e^{j(\phi+\omega t)}$ or $e^{j(\omega t+\phi)}$.

sections.learning_goal: Read a fixed phasor's magnitude and angle as its real-axis projection.
